findings.bug: The lastIndexOf loop uses condition `i > 0`, so index 0 is never examined and an element stored at index 0 is reported as not found (-1).
findings.why_real: The java.util.List#lastIndexOf contract requires returning the highest index i with Objects.equals(o, get(i)) or -1 if absent; the sibling indexOf on line 52 correctly iterates `i < len` covering index 0. The `i > 0` bound is an off-by-one that excludes index 0.
findings.how_to_prove: new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"a"}).lastIndexOf("a") -> expected 0, actual -1. Also new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"x","y"}).lastIndexOf("x") -> expected 0, actual -1.

findings.bug: equals is asymmetric and throws on a valid List argument: an ordinary List (e.g. ArrayList) compared TO an ImmutableList invokes AbstractList.equals which calls listIterator() on the ImmutableList, which throws UnsupportedOperationException.
findings.why_real: Object#equals requires symmetry: a.equals(b) == b.equals(a). AbstractList.equals(Object o) is implemented as `ListIterator e1 = listIterator(); ListIterator e2 = ((List)o).listIterator(); ...` — it calls listIterator() on the OTHER list. ImmutableList#listIterator() (line 197) throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the reverse comparison throws on valid input instead of returning true.
findings.how_to_prove: List<String> a = new ArrayList<>(java.util.Arrays.asList("a","b")); List<String> b = new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"a","b"}); assertTrue(b.equals(a)) passes, but a.equals(b) throws UnsupportedOperationException instead of returning true (violates equals symmetry).

findings.bug: The Comparator returns -2 for CONFLICT for BOTH compare(a,b) and compare(b,a) when two types conflict (conflict is symmetric), so signum(compare(a,b)) == signum(compare(b,a)) == -1, violating the antisymmetry requirement.
findings.why_real: java.util.Comparator#compare contract requires signum(compare(x,y)) == -signum(compare(y,x)) for all x,y. compareTypes yields CONFLICT symmetrically (e.g. an object type vs a primitive type both map to CONFLICT via the symmetric branches at lines 100-105), and compare maps CONFLICT to -2 unconditionally, so both directions return a negative value rather than negatives of each other. This can trigger TimSort's 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' IllegalArgumentException when sorting collections containing conflicting types.
findings.how_to_prove: Take two conflicting ArgTypes t1 (an object) and t2 (a primitive int). comparator.compare(t1,t2) returns -2 and comparator.compare(t2,t1) also returns -2; assert Integer.signum(compare(t1,t2)) == -Integer.signum(compare(t2,t1)) fails (both -1).
